reading_passages.title: How Honey Is Made
reading_passages.body:
Honey begins its life as nectar, a sweet, watery liquid that bees patiently gather from deep inside flowers. A single worker bee may visit hundreds of separate blooms in a single day. It sucks up the nectar and carries it all the way home inside a special stomach kept just for the purpose, quite separate from the ordinary stomach it uses for its own food.

Back at the hive, the real work begins in earnest. The bee passes the nectar mouth to mouth to other waiting workers, who then pass it on again, over and over, in a long relay. As it travels from bee to bee, natural substances are slowly added to it and it begins to change and thicken. The bees then spread the half-made honey into the six-sided wax cells of the honeycomb and beat their wings hard, all together, like hundreds of tiny fans, driving off most of the water until what remains is thick, golden and ready.

Once the honey is finally ready, the bees seal each cell with a small, neat lid of wax to keep it perfectly fresh, sometimes for years on end. A sealed honeycomb is one of the very few foods that almost never goes off. It is slow, patient, astonishing teamwork: a single honeybee makes only a tiny amount of honey — less than one teaspoonful — in its entire short life. This means that the full jar standing on your breakfast table really represents the lifetime work of hundreds and hundreds of bees, all working quietly together for the good of the whole hive.

reading_passages.title: The Man Who Grows Forests on Rooftops
reading_passages.topic: Our Beautiful World — greening the city
reading_passages.instructions: Read the article about Daniel Owusu, then choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) for each question.
reading_passages.body:
When Daniel Owusu tells people he is a farmer, they picture open fields. In fact his farms sit on the flat roofs of office blocks and car parks in the centre of one of the busiest cities in West Africa.

Owusu trained as an architect, not a gardener. For years he designed glass towers like everyone else, until a long illness forced him to spend months indoors looking out over a grey sea of concrete. 'I realised I had helped build a city with almost nowhere for anything green to live,' he says. 'I had been part of the problem.'

His idea was simple but stubborn: every unused roof, he argued, was a field waiting to happen. Persuading building owners was harder. Many feared the weight of the soil, or leaks, or the cost. Owusu's answer was to start small and let the results speak. He covered one modest rooftop with lightweight beds of vegetables and herbs, tended by people from the neighbourhood, and invited sceptical landlords to come and see.

The rooftop did more than grow food. In summer the planted roof kept the floor below it noticeably cooler, cutting the building's air-conditioning bills. Rainwater that had once rushed straight into overloaded drains was now soaked up by the soil. Bees and birds, almost unknown in the district, began to return. What had looked like charity turned out to make hard financial sense.

Today more than forty roofs across the city are under cultivation, and a waiting list of owners want to join. Owusu is careful, though, not to promise too much. 'A few gardens will not undo what cities have done to the natural world,' he warns. 'But they change how people think. Once someone has grown a tomato above the traffic, they never look at a bare roof the same way again. That shift in the mind is the real harvest.'

reading_passages.title: The Return of the School Garden
reading_passages.body:
A growing number of schools, in towns and cities alike, are turning unused corners of their grounds into thriving vegetable gardens, and the reasons go well beyond simply growing a few rows of carrots.

The most obvious benefit is food. Pupils who have grown a vegetable themselves, all the way from a tiny seed, are far more willing to taste it at last, and along the way they learn where their everyday meals actually come from. Teachers report that even the fussiest eaters become noticeably more adventurous at lunchtime once they have proudly dug up their own muddy potatoes.

There are quieter, gentler benefits too. Many pupils describe the garden as the calmest part of their entire week, a green and welcome escape from the noise and rush of the busy classroom. Staff have noticed, again and again, that anxious or restless children often settle almost at once when they are given a simple, repetitive task to do with their hands, such as watering, weeding or gently raking the soil.

Gardens also teach valuable skills that are very hard to deliver from a textbook alone. Planting seeds and then waiting for the harvest demand real patience, because nothing in a garden can ever be hurried along. Working together on a shared plot quietly forces pupils to cooperate and to divide up the many jobs fairly between them. And the whole garden becomes a living science lesson, where dry ideas about soil, weather, bees and insects suddenly feel real and important.

Finally, school gardens cut waste in a satisfying circle. Vegetable peelings and grass cuttings go straight onto a compost heap rather than into a bin, slowly rotting down into rich, dark food for the crop the following year.

reading_passages.title: The Plants That Break the Rules
reading_passages.topic: Our Beautiful World — extraordinary plant life
reading_passages.instructions: Read the article about four unusual plants and answer the questions. Write a short answer (a few words) for each.
reading_passages.body:
We tend to think of plants as quiet, patient things that stay where they are put. A few species, however, seem determined to break every rule we expect them to follow.

Take the welwitschia, which grows in the Namib Desert of southern Africa. It produces only two leaves in its entire life, yet it can live for more than a thousand years. The leaves never fall; instead they grow steadily, split and fray at the tips until the plant looks like a tangled heap of old ribbon. Botanists call it a living fossil, because it has barely changed in millions of years.

Far to the east, in the rainforests of Sumatra, the titan arum takes a different approach to survival. Once every few years it unfurls a flower taller than an adult, which gives off a powerful smell of rotting meat. Visitors often hold their noses, but the stink is no accident: it draws in the flies and beetles that the plant depends on to carry its pollen. The bloom lasts barely two days before it collapses.

The resurrection plant is stranger still. During a drought it curls into a dry, brown ball that looks completely dead and can be blown across the ground by the wind. Yet add a little water and, within hours, it unrolls and turns green again, as though nothing had happened. Some specimens have been brought back to life after decades on a shelf.

Perhaps the boldest of all is the dancing plant of South Asia, whose small side-leaves twitch and rotate in response to warmth, light and even music. Nobody is quite sure why it moves; one theory is that the motion helps the plant find the brightest patches of sun.

What these plants share is a refusal to be ordinary. Each has found an unusual answer to the same question every living thing must face: how to survive.

reading_passages.title: Why Leaves Change Colour
reading_passages.body:
Why do the leaves of so many trees blaze into gold and red each autumn before they finally fall? The answer lies in a green substance called chlorophyll, which fills the leaves all summer long. Chlorophyll has one vital job: it uses the energy in sunlight to make food for the whole tree, and in doing so it also gives the leaves their familiar green colour that we see from spring right through to the end of summer. A single large tree may carry hundreds of thousands of these tiny green food factories.

As autumn slowly arrives, the days grow shorter and cooler, and there is less and less sunlight for the leaves to work with. Sensing the change in the light, the tree gradually stops making chlorophyll, since it is no longer worth the effort. As the strong green colour quietly fades away, the yellow and orange shades that were hidden underneath the green all along are revealed at last. In certain trees the leaves also turn a brilliant, fiery red, and this colour is different: it is one the tree actually makes fresh, from sugar trapped inside the dying leaf.

There is a very practical reason behind all of this beauty. Broad, flat leaves would lose far too much water in the dry winter air, and would be battered and torn by the winter storms, so the tree carefully drops them to save precious water and energy through the cold, dark months ahead. Through the whole of winter the bare tree simply rests, doing almost nothing at all, waiting patiently until the warmth and the light return in spring and the new buds open once again.

reading_passages.title: Four Great Journeys
reading_passages.instructions: Read about four migrating animals (A, B, C and D). For each question, choose the correct animal. You may use each letter more than once.
reading_passages.body:
A  The Arctic tern
No animal travels further. Each year the Arctic tern flies from the Arctic, where it breeds, all the way to the seas around Antarctica and back — a round trip of around 70,000 kilometres. Because it follows the summer at both ends of the planet, it sees more daylight than any other creature on Earth. It rarely lands, snatching fish from the surface of the sea as it goes, and a single tern may cover three million kilometres in its lifetime.

B  The monarch butterfly
The monarch's journey is remarkable not for its length but for who completes it. No single butterfly makes the whole trip from Canada to the forests of central Mexico. Instead the migration is shared across several generations: the butterflies that finally arrive in Mexico are the great-grandchildren of those that first set out. How they find a forest none of them has ever seen remains one of nature's great puzzles.

C  The humpback whale
Humpback whales swim from the cold, food-rich waters near the poles to warm tropical seas where their calves are born. They make the journey without eating at all, living off the fat they built up over the summer. Along the way the males sing long, complex songs that travel for many kilometres underwater; the same song spreads slowly from group to group until whole oceans seem to share a single tune.

D  The wildebeest
On the plains of East Africa more than a million wildebeest move in a vast circle, always chasing the rain and the fresh grass it brings. There is no leader; the herd simply turns as one when the weather changes. The most dangerous moments come at the rivers, where crocodiles wait, and only the animals that cross quickly and together are likely to survive.

reading_passages.title: The River That Came Back to Life
reading_passages.instructions: Read the article about a town that restored its river, then complete the notes below. Write one to four words in each gap.
reading_passages.body:
Thirty years ago the River Mell, which runs through the small town of Casterton, was little more than an open drain. Factories upstream had poured waste into it for decades, the water ran a strange grey-green, and the fish had long since disappeared. Most residents simply kept their backs to it.

The change began with a single retired teacher, Pamela Osei, who started picking litter from the banks on her morning walks. Neighbours who had once ignored the river began to join her, and within a year a small volunteer group had formed. They called themselves the River Watch.

Their first victory was information. By testing the water themselves and sharing the results online, they put quiet pressure on the factories until two of the worst polluters agreed to install filters. Cleaner water alone, however, was not enough. The group also planted reeds along the banks, which trap dirt and give insects and birds somewhere to shelter, and they removed several old concrete walls so that the river could spread into its natural floodplain after heavy rain.

Slowly, life returned. Dragonflies appeared first, then small fish, and three years ago an otter — an animal not seen in Casterton for half a century — was photographed at dawn. The town now holds a River Festival every spring, and local schools use the banks as an outdoor classroom.

Pamela is modest about her part. 'I never set out to start a movement,' she says. 'I just couldn't walk past the mess any more. The lesson, if there is one, is that a place only stays neglected for as long as nobody decides to care for it.'

reading_passages.title: Why Birds Migrate
reading_passages.body:
As the seasons slowly change, huge numbers of birds set off on some of the most remarkable journeys in all of nature. The main reason they migrate is to find food: when winter strips the trees bare and freezes the hard ground, the insects and seeds quietly vanish, and so many birds fly off to warmer places where food is still plentiful and the days are longer and brighter.

These journeys can be truly astonishing. Some tiny birds, no heavier than a letter, fly thousands of kilometres without ever once stopping to rest. To find their way across wide oceans and empty deserts they have no maps at all to guide them, and yet they rarely get lost. Instead they use a clever mixture of clues — the position of the sun by day and the stars by night, familiar coastlines and mountain ranges far below, and a mysterious natural force called magnetism, which they can somehow sense and which acts like an invisible map inside their heads.

Birds very often travel together in a great group, taking turns at the tiring front position while the others rest in the slipstream behind, because flying together in this way saves a huge amount of precious energy. Most follow exactly the same routes year after year, generation after generation, passing over the very same fields and rivers that their parents and grandparents crossed before them. It is not an easy or a safe trip, though, by any means: migration is also extremely dangerous, with storms, exhaustion, hunger and hungry predators all along the way, and sadly many birds do not survive to see the journey through to its end.

reading_passages.title: The Return of the Wolves
reading_passages.instructions: Read the article about wolves in Yellowstone, then complete the notes below. Use NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each gap.
reading_passages.body:
When the last wolves were hunted out of Yellowstone National Park in the 1920s, few people thought it mattered. The park looked beautiful without them. Yet over the following seventy years, scientists watched something strange and worrying happen to the whole landscape.

With no wolves to hunt them, the number of elk grew enormously. These large deer ate young trees faster than the trees could grow. Along the rivers, the willows and aspens that once lined the banks almost disappeared. Without those trees, songbirds lost their nesting places, and beavers, which need willow to build with, became rare.

In 1995, after years of debate, scientists released fourteen wolves back into the park. What followed surprised even the experts. The wolves, of course, killed some elk, but the bigger effect was on how the elk behaved. The deer no longer dared to linger in the open river valleys where they could be caught. They began to move more, and to avoid the most dangerous places altogether.

Freed from constant grazing, the young trees finally grew tall. As the willows returned, so did the songbirds. Beavers came back too, and their dams created ponds that gave homes to fish, frogs and insects. Even the rivers changed shape: the new plants held the banks together, so the water ran in steadier channels instead of washing the soil away.

Scientists call this a "trophic cascade" — a chain of effects that begins with one species at the top and ripples all the way down. The story of Yellowstone taught ecologists an important lesson: a single missing animal can quietly change an entire ecosystem, and bringing it back can heal far more than anyone expects.

reading_passages.title: A Weekend in the National Park
reading_passages.body:
Last weekend, my family visited a national park about two hours from our city. We arrived early in the morning, before it got too hot. The park was full of tall trees, colourful birds, and a river that ran through the middle of it.

We walked along a marked trail for about an hour. Our guide told us the names of different plants and pointed out animal tracks in the mud. Halfway through the walk, we stopped by the river to eat lunch and watch the water flow over the rocks.

In the afternoon, we visited the park's small information centre, where we learned about the animals that live in the area, including deer, foxes, and many kinds of birds. By the time we left, everyone was tired but happy. My little sister said it was the best day of her holiday so far.

reading_passages.title: Growing Vegetables on a Windowsill
reading_passages.instructions: Imagine you are giving a short talk about growing vegetables on a windowsill. Use the article to make short notes under each heading.
reading_passages.body:
You don't need a garden to grow your own vegetables. A bright windowsill and a few containers are enough to keep a kitchen supplied with fresh herbs and salad leaves for much of the year — and it costs very little to begin.

The most important thing is light. A windowsill that faces the sun and receives at least six hours of light a day will grow almost anything; a darker one will only suit a few leafy plants. If your room is dim, a cheap clip-on lamp can make up the difference.

Almost any container will do, from a proper plant pot to an old tin, as long as it has holes in the bottom so that water can escape. Without drainage, the roots sit in water and quickly rot. Stand the containers on a tray to protect the windowsill.

Beginners should start with herbs such as basil and mint, and fast salad leaves like rocket, which are difficult to kill and ready to eat within weeks. Tomatoes and peppers are possible but need more light and patience, so they are better left until you have some experience.

Watering is where most people go wrong. Rather than watering a little every day, wait until the top of the soil feels dry to the touch, then water well. Plants on a windowsill also tend to lean towards the glass, so turn the containers every few days to keep them growing straight. Once the first proper leaves appear, a weak liquid feed every two weeks will keep them strong.

The commonest problem indoors is simply too little light, which makes plants pale and weak. If that happens, move them closer to the window or add a lamp.

listening_tracks.instructions: You will hear a park ranger talk about turning an ordinary garden into a home for wildlife. Complete the notes below. Write one to three words in each gap. You will hear the talk twice.

Hello everyone, and thanks for coming along. People often think you need a huge space to help wildlife, but even a small garden can make a real difference. Let me give you a few simple steps.

listening_tracks.title: Exercise 5 — Interview with a Marine Biologist
listening_tracks.instructions: You will hear an interview with Dr Maya Reyes, a marine biologist who studies ocean plastic. Choose the correct answer (A, B or C) for each question. You will hear the interview twice.
listening_tracks.script_text:
Interviewer: Dr Reyes, when did you first realise plastic was such a problem?
Dr Reyes: Honestly, not in a laboratory at all. I was diving on a reef I'd known for years, and I saw a turtle completely tangled in a shopping bag. That image has stayed with me ever since.
Interviewer: A lot of people picture huge floating islands of rubbish. Is that an accurate image?
Dr Reyes: That's actually the myth I most want to correct. The really dangerous plastic isn't the big, visible stuff — it's the tiny pieces, smaller than a grain of rice, that fish swallow and that work their way right up the food chain.
Interviewer: So the worst of the problem is almost invisible?
Dr Reyes: Exactly. And that's precisely what makes it so hard to make people care — you simply can't photograph it easily.
Interviewer: Whose responsibility is it to fix — shoppers, or companies?
Dr Reyes: People always want me to blame the shopper. But asking individuals to solve this on their own is unfair; the real change has to come from the companies that produce all the packaging in the first place.
Interviewer: Is it too late?
Dr Reyes: No — and I'm always careful to say so. The ocean recovers surprisingly fast when we give it the chance. In places where fishing was paused, the reefs came back within just a few years.
Interviewer: What's the one thing you'd ask our listeners to do?
Dr Reyes: Please don't feel guilty — guilt just makes people switch off. I'd far rather they picked one piece of single-use plastic they use every day, and simply refused it. Start there.

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: The Man Who Grows Forests on Rooftops
listening_tracks.script_text:
When Daniel Owusu tells people he is a farmer, they picture open fields. In fact his farms sit on the flat roofs of office blocks and car parks in the centre of one of the busiest cities in West Africa.

Owusu trained as an architect, not a gardener. For years he designed glass towers like everyone else, until a long illness forced him to spend months indoors looking out over a grey sea of concrete. 'I realised I had helped build a city with almost nowhere for anything green to live,' he says. 'I had been part of the problem.'

His idea was simple but stubborn: every unused roof, he argued, was a field waiting to happen. Persuading building owners was harder. Many feared the weight of the soil, or leaks, or the cost. Owusu's answer was to start small and let the results speak. He covered one modest rooftop with lightweight beds of vegetables and herbs, tended by people from the neighbourhood, and invited sceptical landlords to come and see.

The rooftop did more than grow food. In summer the planted roof kept the floor below it noticeably cooler, cutting the building's air-conditioning bills. Rainwater that had once rushed straight into overloaded drains was now soaked up by the soil. Bees and birds, almost unknown in the district, began to return. What had looked like charity turned out to make hard financial sense.

Today more than forty roofs across the city are under cultivation, and a waiting list of owners want to join. Owusu is careful, though, not to promise too much. 'A few gardens will not undo what cities have done to the natural world,' he warns. 'But they change how people think. Once someone has grown a tomato above the traffic, they never look at a bare roof the same way again. That shift in the mind is the real harvest.'

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: The Plants That Break the Rules
listening_tracks.script_text:
We tend to think of plants as quiet, patient things that stay where they are put. A few species, however, seem determined to break every rule we expect them to follow.

Take the welwitschia, which grows in the Namib Desert of southern Africa. It produces only two leaves in its entire life, yet it can live for more than a thousand years. The leaves never fall; instead they grow steadily, split and fray at the tips until the plant looks like a tangled heap of old ribbon. Botanists call it a living fossil, because it has barely changed in millions of years.

Far to the east, in the rainforests of Sumatra, the titan arum takes a different approach to survival. Once every few years it unfurls a flower taller than an adult, which gives off a powerful smell of rotting meat. Visitors often hold their noses, but the stink is no accident: it draws in the flies and beetles that the plant depends on to carry its pollen. The bloom lasts barely two days before it collapses.

The resurrection plant is stranger still. During a drought it curls into a dry, brown ball that looks completely dead and can be blown across the ground by the wind. Yet add a little water and, within hours, it unrolls and turns green again, as though nothing had happened. Some specimens have been brought back to life after decades on a shelf.

Perhaps the boldest of all is the dancing plant of South Asia, whose small side-leaves twitch and rotate in response to warmth, light and even music. Nobody is quite sure why it moves; one theory is that the motion helps the plant find the brightest patches of sun.

What these plants share is a refusal to be ordinary. Each has found an unusual answer to the same question every living thing must face: how to survive.

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: The River That Came Back to Life
listening_tracks.script_text:
Thirty years ago the River Mell, which runs through the small town of Casterton, was little more than an open drain. Factories upstream had poured waste into it for decades, the water ran a strange grey-green, and the fish had long since disappeared. Most residents simply kept their backs to it.

The change began with a single retired teacher, Pamela Osei, who started picking litter from the banks on her morning walks. Neighbours who had once ignored the river began to join her, and within a year a small volunteer group had formed. They called themselves the River Watch.

Their first victory was information. By testing the water themselves and sharing the results online, they put quiet pressure on the factories until two of the worst polluters agreed to install filters. Cleaner water alone, however, was not enough. The group also planted reeds along the banks, which trap dirt and give insects and birds somewhere to shelter, and they removed several old concrete walls so that the river could spread into its natural floodplain after heavy rain.

Slowly, life returned. Dragonflies appeared first, then small fish, and three years ago an otter — an animal not seen in Casterton for half a century — was photographed at dawn. The town now holds a River Festival every spring, and local schools use the banks as an outdoor classroom.

Pamela is modest about her part. 'I never set out to start a movement,' she says. 'I just couldn't walk past the mess any more. The lesson, if there is one, is that a place only stays neglected for as long as nobody decides to care for it.'

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: Four Great Journeys
listening_tracks.script_text:
A  The Arctic tern
No animal travels further. Each year the Arctic tern flies from the Arctic, where it breeds, all the way to the seas around Antarctica and back — a round trip of around 70,000 kilometres. Because it follows the summer at both ends of the planet, it sees more daylight than any other creature on Earth. It rarely lands, snatching fish from the surface of the sea as it goes, and a single tern may cover three million kilometres in its lifetime.

B  The monarch butterfly
The monarch's journey is remarkable not for its length but for who completes it. No single butterfly makes the whole trip from Canada to the forests of central Mexico. Instead the migration is shared across several generations: the butterflies that finally arrive in Mexico are the great-grandchildren of those that first set out. How they find a forest none of them has ever seen remains one of nature's great puzzles.

C  The humpback whale
Humpback whales swim from the cold, food-rich waters near the poles to warm tropical seas where their calves are born. They make the journey without eating at all, living off the fat they built up over the summer. Along the way the males sing long, complex songs that travel for many kilometres underwater; the same song spreads slowly from group to group until whole oceans seem to share a single tune.

D  The wildebeest
On the plains of East Africa more than a million wildebeest move in a vast circle, always chasing the rain and the fresh grass it brings. There is no leader; the herd simply turns as one when the weather changes. The most dangerous moments come at the rivers, where crocodiles wait, and only the animals that cross quickly and together are likely to survive.

writing_tasks.model_answer:
Restoring the River Mell: A Proposal for the Council

Introduction
This report examines the condition of the River Mell and recommends how it could be restored.

Current problems
For many years the river has been neglected. Waste was allowed to enter the water from factories upstream, and as a result the fish disappeared and the banks were left covered in litter. At present the river is avoided by most residents rather than enjoyed.

Proposed action
Several steps could be taken to improve the situation. First, the water should be tested regularly, and the results should be made public so that polluters can be held responsible. Reeds could be planted along the banks, where dirt is trapped and wildlife is sheltered. Old concrete walls could also be removed so that the river is allowed to spread naturally after heavy rain.

Benefits
If these measures are carried out, the river will gradually be restored. A valuable habitat would be created, pollution would fall, and the area could be enjoyed by schools and families. Such conservation work is also sustainable, since a healthy river needs little maintenance once it has recovered.

Recommendation
It is therefore recommended that the council approve the restoration as soon as possible.

discussion_how.q: Why do you think some people find nature boring while others love it?
discussion_how.how: Give a reason for each side — don't just pick one. Maybe some grew up outdoors, while others never had the chance. 'It often depends on what you were shown as a child.' Show you can see why both feel the way they do.

discussion_how.q: Are zoos and botanical gardens a good way to learn about nature, or not?
discussion_how.how: Take a clear view, then justify it. 'Yes — for many people, it's the only way they'll ever see these species up close.' Or push the other way: animals in cages aren't truly wild. Pick a side and give one solid reason.

discussion_how.q: Should children spend more time outdoors learning about plants and animals?
discussion_how.how: Give a recommendation, and say what would come of it. 'Yes — children who explore outdoors grow up caring more about nature.' Back your yes or no with the result it would bring. That outcome is what makes the case.

card_points_how.how: Bring it to life — don't just name it, describe it so I can picture it. Shape, size, colour, the one feature that stands out. 'A chameleon, with eyes that swivel in different directions.' Pick the detail that makes it unforgettable.
card_points_how.point: a plant or animal you find fascinating, and what it looks like

card_points_how.how: Now how it lives — how does it survive where it's found? Talk about its habitat and one clever way it copes. How does it find food, hide from a predator, or handle the cold? 'It blends in so well that predators swim right past.' Show what makes it a survivor.
card_points_how.point: how it survives in its habitat

card_points_how.how: This is the compare step — set it against something ordinary. Comparatives do the work here: 'An octopus is far smarter than most fish.' Or go superlative: 'It's the most resourceful creature in the rock pool.' The contrast is what makes it stand out.
card_points_how.point: how it compares with a more ordinary plant or animal

card_points_how.how: Now give your view — do people notice nature enough, or not? Back it with what you see: phones over parks, or a real love of the outdoors? 'Most people walk past amazing things without looking.' Take a side, and say why.
card_points_how.point: whether people pay enough attention to the natural world around them

card_points_how.how: Close on why it matters to you — the personal note. Not 'it's interesting', but what it makes you feel or think. 'It reminds me how much we still don't understand.' End on something real, so the talk lands.
card_points_how.point: why this plant or animal matters to you

assessed.what: A developed, fluent 1-2 minute long turn — describe, compare, and evaluate (D-C-E), not just a flat description.
Justify your views in the discussion and respond to follow-ups — not just agree.
Clear pronunciation and intonation; a steady pace; sensible stress.

pitfalls: Only describing — the card also asks you to compare and evaluate (D-C-E).
One-word answers in the long turn (kills S1 fluency) — develop every point.
Listing facts with no reaction — say why it fascinates you (the evaluate move).
Finishing under a minute, or rushing your delivery (S3).

speaking_tasks.model_response: One creature I find fascinating is the welwitschia — well, it's actually a plant, not an animal. It looks like a tangled heap of old leaves, far stranger than any normal plant. It survives in one of the driest habitats on Earth, because it can live for over a thousand years on almost no water, which makes it one of the toughest species I know. Compared with an ordinary garden flower, it is much less pretty but far more impressive. I don't think most people pay enough attention to nature like this; they walk past amazing things every day without noticing them.

speaking_tasks.title: Nature in the city
speaking_tasks.intro: We'll now discuss some broader questions related to the topic.
discussion_questions: Should every new building be required to include green space?
Are rooftop gardens and city farms worth the cost and effort?
Is it more important for a city to be green or to be affordable?

frame.name: P-R-R-E
frame.example: Turning an empty, derelict lot into a community garden transforms a neighbourhood (Point), because it gives people a green place to meet, grow food and relax (Reason), so a forgotten corner becomes the heart of the street (Result) — in cities around the world, neighbours have turned weed-filled lots into gardens full of vegetables and bees (Example).

examples: If you ask me, the answer is clearly ___.
The main reason I think so is that ___.

decode.plain: Discuss bringing nature into cities — take a position, give reasons, and respond with balance.

discussion_how.q: Should every new building be required to include green space?
discussion_how.how: Give a recommendation, and say what would result. 'Yes — if every building added green space, whole cities would breathe easier.' Back your yes or no with the effect it brings. That outcome is what makes the case.

discussion_how.q: Are rooftop gardens and city farms worth the cost and effort?
discussion_how.how: Weigh the worth against the cost — that's the heart of this one. 'They cost a lot, but they grow food and cool buildings — a sustainable use of scarce space.' Don't just say good or bad; show the trade-off, then judge it.

discussion_how.q: Is it more important for a city to be green or to be affordable?
discussion_how.how: Take a side on the trade-off, but show you see the tension. 'Affordable first — people need homes before parks.' Then a balance turn: 'That said, green and affordable don't have to fight; good planning gives both.' Pick a side, then soften fairly.

card_points_how.how: Open by saying where you stand — clearly, in one line. Don't list every angle first; lead with your view. 'I think every city needs far more green space.' A firm opening gives the rest something to build on.

Now your strongest reason — one, developed fully, not a list. Make the point, say why, show what follows, give an example. 'Green space cools a city and lifts people's mood, so everyone lives better.' One deep reason beats five quick ones.

Back it with something concrete — an example, or a comparison. Compare a grey concrete street with one lined with trees. Or point to a city that built parks and saw life improve. A real case is far more convincing than a general claim.
card_points_how.point: add an example or a comparison

card_points_how.how: Show you've weighed both sides — concede a point, once. 'That said, land in a city is expensive, and housing matters too.' One fair concession makes you sound balanced, not one-sided.

assessed.what: A developed, fluent turn — ideas extended, not one-word answers.
You justify opinions and respond to the examiner in the discussion — not just agree.
Clear pronunciation and intonation; a steady pace; sensible stress.

pitfalls: One-word answers (kills S1 fluency) — develop every point.
Listing points with no reasons — give a reason and an example.
Just agreeing in the discussion — justify and add something (S2).
Finishing too quickly, or rushing your delivery (S3).

speaking_tasks.model_response: Where I live there isn't much green space, just a few small parks. One idea I like is the rooftop garden, where vegetables are grown on the roofs of ordinary buildings. The process is simple: lightweight beds are added, crops are cultivated by local people, and rainwater is soaked up instead of overloading the drainage. As a result, the building is kept cooler and a new habitat is created for bees and birds. I don't think a city can ever be perfect for the environment, but it can certainly be made far more sustainable than it is today.

speaking_tasks.title: Looking after a natural place
speaking_tasks.intro: We'll now discuss some broader questions related to the topic.
discussion_questions: Whose job is it to protect the environment — governments, companies, or individuals?
Are volunteer groups an effective way to look after local nature?
Should people be fined for dropping litter in natural places?

frame.name: P-R-R-E
frame.example: When a community cleans up its local river, everyone benefits (Point), because a clean river brings back fish, birds and clean water (Reason), so the whole neighbourhood has a healthier, nicer place to live (Result) — in many towns, volunteers who gave up a few weekends turned a rubbish-filled stream into a place children play again (Example).

examples: If you ask me, the answer is clearly ___.
The main reason I think so is that ___.

decode.plain: Discuss looking after natural places — take a position, give reasons, and respond with balance.

discussion_how.q: Whose job is it to protect the environment — governments, companies, or individuals?
discussion_how.how: Take a side — or share it out, but clearly. 'Mostly governments, because only they can make rules that stick.' You can apportion: a bit to each, but say who carries the most. Back your split with a reason, don't just list all three.

discussion_how.q: Are volunteer groups an effective way to look after local nature?
discussion_how.how: Give a view, then show what volunteers actually achieve. 'Yes — a local group can clear a river that no one else will touch.' A real example of their impact is what proves the point. Effective or not, back it with what you've seen.

discussion_how.q: Should people be fined for dropping litter in natural places?
discussion_how.how: Give a recommendation, and say what would result. 'Yes — fines make people think twice, so places stay cleaner.' A balance turn fits well here: 'That said, teaching people why may work better than punishing them.' Recommend, then show the effect.

card_points_how.how: Open by saying where you stand — in one clear line. Don't drift through every angle first; lead with your position. 'I think we're all responsible for protecting natural places.' A firm opening gives the rest something to build on.

Now your strongest reason — one, built out fully, not a list. Make the point, say why, show what follows, give an example. 'If no one looks after a place, it slowly falls apart — and once it's gone, it's gone.' One deep reason beats five quick ones.

Back it with something real — an example, or a comparison. Point to a beach cleanup, or a forest left to ruin versus one that's cared for. A concrete case makes your point far more convincing than a general claim.
card_points_how.point: add an example or a comparison

card_points_how.how: Show you've weighed both sides — concede a point, once. 'That said, ordinary people can't do it alone — governments have to help.' One fair concession makes you sound balanced, not preachy.

Finishing too quickly, or rushing your delivery (S3).

speaking_tasks.model_response: There's a small river near my home that was badly neglected for years. The situation was poor: waste had been allowed into the water and the fish had disappeared. Then several things were done by a local volunteer group — the banks were cleared, the water was tested, and reeds were planted. As a result, wildlife has slowly returned and the restoration is still going on. I think everyone shares responsibility for conservation, but I really do believe small actions make a difference, because once one person starts caring for a place, others usually join in.

speaking_tasks.title: A journey in nature
speaking_tasks.intro: We'll now discuss some broader questions related to the topic.
discussion_questions: Is it better to see wildlife in real life or in high-quality films?
Should humans do more to protect the routes that migrating animals use?
Why are people so fascinated by long animal journeys?

frame.name: P-R-R-E
frame.example: The Arctic tern makes the most astonishing journey of any animal (Point), because it flies from the Arctic right down to the Antarctic and back each year (Reason), so it chases an endless summer across the whole planet (Result) — in a lifetime, one bird travels further than to the Moon and back (Example).

examples: If you ask me, the answer is clearly ___.
The main reason I think so is that ___.

decode.plain: Discuss animal journeys and nature — take a clear position, back it with reasons, and respond with balance.

discussion_how.q: Is it better to see wildlife in real life or in high-quality films?
discussion_how.how: Take a side, then compare the two directly. 'Real life wins — a film can't match standing metres from a wild animal.' Weigh what each gives: films reach everyone, but real life is unforgettable. A clear comparison is what answers this well.

discussion_how.q: Should humans do more to protect the routes that migrating animals use?
discussion_how.how: Give a recommendation, and say what it would lead to. 'Yes — if we protect their routes, whole species can survive.' Back your yes or no with the result it brings. That outcome is what makes the case strong.

discussion_how.q: Why are people so fascinated by long animal journeys?
discussion_how.how: Offer a reason — and you can give more than one. Maybe it's the mystery of how they navigate, or that it makes our own travels look small. 'These journeys remind us nature can do what we can't.' A thoughtful reason matters more than a quick answer.

card_points_how.how: Start by saying where you stand — clearly, in one line. Don't be vague or list every angle first; lead with your view. 'I think protecting migration routes should come first.' A clear opening gives the rest something to build on.
Now your strongest reason — one, developed fully, not a quick list. Build it out: make the point, say why, show what follows, give an example. One reason taken deep beats five mentioned in passing.

Back it with something concrete — a real example, or a comparison. Compare animal travel with our own: birds that navigate across oceans with no map. Or set real life against a film. A vivid example makes your point stick in the listener's mind.
card_points_how.point: add an example or a comparison

card_points_how.how: Show you've thought about both sides — concede a point, once. 'That said, films can reach people who'll never travel.' Or: 'It depends on what you want — wonder, or convenience.' One fair concession makes you sound balanced, not stubborn.

speaking_tasks.model_response: The journey I find most remarkable is the migration of the Arctic tern, which flies almost from pole to pole every year. It's far more impressive than any human journey, because the bird navigates thousands of kilometres entirely on its own, with no map and no rest. What makes it so difficult is that predators and storms wait the whole way. Compared with the way we travel, by plane in a few comfortable hours, it seems almost unbelievable. I think documentaries are a brilliant way to experience journeys like this, although seeing even one wild bird in real life is more exciting than any screen.

speaking_tasks.title: Speaking Part 1 — Interview (nature & the outdoors)
speaking_tasks.intro: The examiner will ask you some questions about yourself. Answer naturally; these are short, familiar-topic questions to warm up.
discussion_questions: Do you enjoy spending time outdoors? What do you like to do?
Is there a natural place near your home that you like?
Do you prefer the countryside or the city? Why?
Have you ever grown a plant or looked after an animal?
Is protecting nature something young people think about where you live?

frame.name: P-R-R-E
frame.example: Instead of just 'yes', try: I really enjoy being outdoors (Point), because it helps me unwind (Reason), so I always feel better afterwards (Result) — last weekend a long walk left me calm and clear (Example).

examples: Yes, and the main reason is ___.
There's a ___ near my home, where I ___.
The place I like best is ___, because ___.
If I had to choose, I'd say ___.

decode.plain: Answer the examiner's warm-up questions on nature and the outdoors — short answers, but extend each with a reason.

discussion_how.q: Do you enjoy spending time outdoors? What do you like to do?
discussion_how.how: Don't stop at 'yes'. Name what you actually do, and say why you like it. 'Yes — I love hiking, because it clears my head after a busy week.' One activity plus one reason turns a flat answer into a real one.

discussion_how.q: Is there a natural place near your home that you like?
discussion_how.how: Name a real place, then one reason it suits you. 'There's a park near my home where I go to relax.' Don't just say 'yes, a park' — add what it gives you. A small detail makes the answer feel genuine.

discussion_how.q: Do you prefer the countryside or the city? Why?
discussion_how.how: State your preference clearly, then justify it briefly. 'The countryside, mainly because it's quieter and I can breathe.' You don't need a speech — one honest reason is enough. 'Mainly because...' is a handy way to start.

discussion_how.q: Have you ever grown a plant or looked after an animal?
discussion_how.how: Answer yes or no, then give a quick real example. 'Yes — I grew tomatoes on our balcony last summer.' Even a small story beats a bare 'yes'. If it's no, say what you'd like to try instead.

discussion_how.q: Is protecting nature something young people think about where you live?
discussion_how.how: Give a view, with a reason — and you can keep it general. 'Some do — many of my friends appreciate wildlife and worry about waste.' You're not speaking for everyone; just say what you notice. A reason makes even a general answer solid.
